notes: Bundler-plugin route: bugseeEsbuildPlugin from @bugsee/bundler-plugin-core stamps debug ids and uploads source maps when the esbuild build ends. esbuild has no config file: the plugin goes into the plugins of the build() or context() call in your own build script, so the wizard hands you the exact snippet instead of editing it (an esbuild CLI command with flags cannot take plugins: move the build into a script that calls the JavaScript API). If you did not set sourcemap the plugin sets 'external'; sourcemap: false leaves nothing to upload and sourcemap: 'inline' writes no map files. The plugin uploads only the bundles and maps of this build (it reads esbuild's metafile and never walks the output folder). It skips builds that NODE_ENV=development marks as development (uploadInDevelopment: true overrides). tsup is NOT covered: tsup tells esbuild not to write and writes the files itself afterwards, so nothing is on disk when the plugin runs; use the bugsee-cli post-build step instead (the manual-upload page of the Bugsee JavaScript docs has the tsup recipe). Angular's builder, Bun's bundler and tsc have no plugin hook either: they use the bugsee-cli script. The plugin reads the app token from BUGSEE_APP_TOKEN. From SDK 0.1.0-beta.7 the plugin also reads the token from .env.bugsee-build-plugin (the file the wizard writes); older SDKs need BUGSEE_APP_TOKEN exported. In CI, export BUGSEE_APP_TOKEN. The plugin does nothing without an app token. By default it deletes the .map files from the build output after a fully successful upload (deleteMaps: false keeps them), so they are not deployed. A build that pins script hashes with Subresource Integrity in its emitted HTML is warned about or refused. Hashes pinned elsewhere, such as in a server-side manifest or a page rendered at request time, are not detected and can break scripts silently: check those builds for integrity pins before enabling the plugin. pnpm 11 approvals: the install script of the plugin's CLI dependency must be approved, and its name depends on the SDK (@bugsee/cli from 0.1.0-beta.7, @bugsee/bugsee-cli before), so both are written to allowBuilds; the one the project does not use is a harmless pre-approval and is removed again by uninstall.
verify: Verify symbolication in a production build: serve or deploy it (not the dev server), trigger a test error from it (for example a button that throws new Error('Bugsee test error')), then open the report in the Bugsee dashboard. The stack should show your original files, functions and lines; minified positions such as a.js:1:48210 mean the source maps were not uploaded for this build or do not match it.
